vignette:
Gerald Marsh is a 71-year-old married man who has worked as a security guard for the better part of four decades, a career built on the quiet conviction that vigilance keeps people safe. Fourteen months ago, that conviction was shattered. Gerald was on duty at a regional transit hub when a coordinated attack unfolded - explosions at two entry points, a surge of panicked commuters, and then a man moving against the crowd with deliberate, terrible purpose. Gerald was among the first personnel on scene. He remembers the smell before the sound registered properly, remembers the specific angle of afternoon light through the shattered glass facade, remembers a face - the attacker's face, turning toward him with an expression Gerald has never been able to name. What followed is something he cannot assemble into a coherent sequence even now. He knows he was thrown. He knows there was a period of time he cannot account for. He knows people died within yards of where he stood. The event does not live in his mind as a story with a beginning, middle, and end; it lives as a collection of images and sensations that arrive without warning and without narrative logic, vivid and overwhelming one moment, then strangely hollow the next, as though he is watching footage of a stranger's worst day.

In the weeks after the attack, Gerald returned to work because he did not know what else to do with himself. The transit hub was a different building now - repaired, repainted - but the work itself had not changed, and that was the problem. Every shift placed him in the middle of crowds of strangers, and Gerald found himself scanning faces with an intensity that exhausted him. He was certain that the capacity for that kind of violence existed in ordinary-looking people, and he had learned, in the worst possible way, that he could not always spot it in time. He began positioning himself at every opportunity - at his post, in the break room, at the diner where he and his wife ate on Sundays - with his back against a wall and a full view of the room in front of him. His wife noticed. She stopped suggesting they sit at certain tables. She stopped asking why.

What has weighed on Gerald most heavily, though, is not the fear but the shame. He had come to believe, with a quiet and corrosive certainty, that a different man - a sharper man, a more experienced man - would have read the situation earlier, moved differently, changed the outcome. He was a security professional. This was precisely the scenario his entire working life had been oriented toward preventing. The sense that he had failed in the one role that mattered most to him had settled into something close to a permanent condition. He spent long hours in the evenings not resting but rehearsing - turning over scenarios in which he confronted the attacker, extracted retribution, restored some balance to a world that felt irreparably tilted. These were not plans so much as compulsions, loops of imagined reckoning that left him no closer to peace.

What frightened him on an ordinary Tuesday, when his granddaughter knocked over a glass at dinner and he felt his hands begin to shake, was not the noise itself but the disproportionality of his own reaction. He had come to believe he could no longer manage even the smallest disruptions without something in him threatening to come apart. He told his wife that evening that he thought he needed to talk to someone, which was the closest Gerald Marsh had come in fourteen months to asking for help.

He presented for his intake appointment wearing his uniform - he had come straight from a shift - and sat in the chair nearest the door with his back against the wall. He was measured and courteous and described events with a flatness that occasionally gave way to something rawer. What he said he was hoping for was to be able to do his job properly again. What he seemed most afraid of was the possibility that the man he was before the attack no longer existed.
